titleStmt.title: Optimizing the Response Time for ROS Tasks in Multi-Core Processors

analytic.title: Optimizing the Response Time for ROS Tasks in Multi-Core Processors

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper presents methods to optimize the response time of ROS (Robot Operating System), a widely utilized open-source meta-operating system in robotic software development. Despite its popularity, ROS lacks real-time capabilities, making it unsuitable for real-time control and difficult to use in embedded systems. Recently, DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) task scheduling algorithms have gained much attention, but they are challenging to apply in the current design of ROS. In this work, we analyze that there are three major challenges in ROS; (i) misalignment delay, (ii) message delivery mechanism using TCP/IP, and (iii) multiple overlapping instances of a single task. We first calculate the new response time bound considering misalignment delay and propose an optimization technique using it to solve the first problem. Furthermore, we address the remaining challenges by assigning priority to the nodes of the DAG and ksoftirqd processes. Our experiments using random tasks show significant improvement, outperforming the state-ofart methods. In addition, our methods are validated through testing autonomous driving software on embedded systems, proving their real-world applicability.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Recently, as many studies on autonomous driving and robots have been conducted, ROS (Robot Operating System), a robot software development tool, is widely used [1], [2]. ROS is open-source, features a vast library, and has a massive global community, including millions of developers. However, ROS has difficulties in satisfying real-time constraints and has clear limitations in its basic structure, which motivated the development of a new type of ROS called ROS2 [3]. Although it has been eight years since ROS2 came out, many developers still use ROS to utilize their libraries [4]. Therefore, there remains a need for methodologies to enhance ROS performance.

A ROS application consists of several independent processes, or nodes, that communicate with each other through topics. To be specific, a publisher node broadcasts a message by publishing data on a specific topic, while a subscriber node listens to the relevant topic periodically. In a typical robotic environment, since information flows from sensor nodes to control nodes, a single directed acyclic graph (DAG) is created by connecting publisher nodes and subscriber nodes as depicted in Fig. 1(a). Some recent studies analyze and reduce the response time of DAG applications [5]- [9]. They assumed that each node moves from a waiting state to a ready state as soon as all predecessor nodes complete execution. In contrast to other DAG tasks, ROS works slightly differently. As depicted in Fig. 1(b), each node in ROS is composed of a default and callback routine. Each node periodically wakes to check the message queue and execute the callback routine if all necessary messages have been received. However, if the callback execution conditions of the node are not satisfied (i.e., if not all the required messages have arrived), only the default routine is executed. In this paper, we refer to this as an asynchronous polling method. Using v 5 , v 6 , and v 7 in Fig. 1(a) as examples, Fig. 1(c) shows the scheduling diagram including the execution of each node and timing parameters. The time at which each node awakens is the polling time, with the interval

Even though v 5 finishes executing, the processor must wait until the next polling time of v 6 , resulting in an additional delay called the misalignment delay. The response time of chain {v 5 , v 6 , v 7 } is the sum of each node's callback execution time, misalignment delay, and preemption delay. Note that in the example shown, the preemption delay is caused by the default routines of other nodes.

This paper addresses a crucial issue in ROS performancethe misalignment delay, which can be adjusted by changing the spinning period of each node. Shortening the spinning period of the node reduces the misalignment delay. However, since the default routine executes at each polling time, the preemption delay caused by the default routine increases. Therefore, assigning each node an appropriate spinning period is important to reduce a task's response time. In order to tackle this challenge, this paper presents an algorithm for assigning spinning periods to nodes that minimize the response time, effectively balancing the misalignment and preemption delays.

ROS uses TCP/IP for inter-node communication, which enables distributed architectures easily [10]. Therefore, communication must be processed between the execution of each node. Otherwise, the subscriber node will not receive the message at the following polling time and will receive the message later, resulting in additional misalignment delays. We solve this challenge by adjusting the priority of threads handling TCP/IP.

Many recent studies on DAG task scheduling assume that the deadline of the task is shorter than its period (D k < T k ), meaning only one task is executed at any given time. However, this assumption may not hold true for embedded systems with low processor performance, as completing a task within its period can be challenging. Additionally, having a task deadline longer than its period does not necessarily make a system unstable or unsafe. For example, in the case of LIDAR sensors, the data publishing period is often between 0.05s and 0.1s, while the reaction times of autonomous vehicles are shown to be longer [11]. Existing heuristic algorithms aimed at reducing response time for DAG tasks assume single-instance cases, which motivated us to propose a new node priority assignment algorithm to improve response time in cases of multiple task instances overlap [7]- [9].

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: In Section II and Section III we present related work and the task model used in this paper. Then, Section IV explains our three optimization methods to solve the challenges mentioned above. Section V presents our experiment results using random tasks and autonomous driving software. Finally, Section VI concludes our paper.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: The response time bounds in multi-core scheduling have been extensively investigated in prior studies [5], [6], [12]. However, these studies do not consider misalignment and preemption delays specific to ROS. Hence, their response time analysis needs to be revised to accommodate ROS. Recent research on response time analysis and scheduling algorithms for ROS2 is also challenging to apply directly to ROS [13], [14]. This is primarily due to significant differences between ROS and ROS2. Firstly, ROS employs TCP/IP for node communication, whereas ROS2 utilizes DDS to enhance real-time capabilities [15]. This results in different communication models, with ROS relying on an asynchronous polling mechanism and ROS2 utilizing an event-triggered mechanism. Furthermore, unlike ROS, which restricts each node to run in a separate process, ROS2 allows multiple nodes to be executed within a single process named an executor, offering greater flexibility for user adjustments.

According to our knowledge, [16] is the only work that addresses misalignment delay, but it assumes critical nodes are not affected by non-critical nodes. In other words, when the critical node finishes execution, the following critical node starts executions regardless of the completion of other noncritical nodes. Since this paper optimized the spin rate only for the critical nodes, there is a limit in improving response time for general cases. Therefore, in this paper, we proposed a spin rate optimization algorithm by combining the new response time bound of ROS and the simulated annealing method to solve the combinatorial optimization problem [17].

Recent scheduling algorithms for multi-core platforms aim to reduce the total response time with static priority scheduling [7]- [9]. Most studies assign higher priority to nodes closer to the source node, preventing subsequent nodes from not being executed due to precedence constraints and reducing the response time. However, this may increase response time in case of multiple simultaneous task instances, which motivated us to derive a new node priority assignment algorithm.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: We consider a ROS system with a single DAG task τ = {T, D, G = (V, E)} on a multi-core platform with m identical cores. T and D denote its spinning period and constrained relative deadline, respectively, and G is a graph defining the set of nodes and edges forming a task. A single task τ infinitely releases a sequence of jobs at every T period, where we express instance number by using the letter k. (i.e. τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ k , ...}) The directed acyclic graph is defined as G = (V, E), where V = {v 1 , v 2 , ..., v n } is a set of nodes and E ⊆ (V × V ) is a set of directed edges. Each node v i ∈ V represents a sequential workload, and an edge (v i , v j ) represents the precedence relation between v i and v j which means v j can only start execution after v i completes. In other words, v i is a predecessor of v j , whereas v j is a successor of v i . The predecessor and successor is defined as

pre(v i ) = {v j ∈ V | (v j , v i ) ∈ E} and succ(v i ) = {v j ∈ V | (v i , v j ) ∈ E}, respectively.
div.p: Without loss of generality, we assume that G has only one source node v src and one sink node v sink . (i.e. v 1 = v src , v 9 = v sink in Fig. 1(a)) As described in Section I, a default routine of each node is always executed at every polling time, but a callback routine may or may not be executed. Therefore, we define two worstcase execution times (WCET) for each node v i ∈ V . DE k,i is WCET when only a default routine is executed, and CE k,i is WCET when a callback is called. For simplicity, the instance number k can be omitted because every instance does the same job. (i.e. DE k,i = DE i , CE k,i = CE i ) Also, each node v i has a spinning period T i and wakes up every T i times to execute the code. Because of this characteristic, every node has a misalignment delay, formally defined as follows.
Definition 1. The misalignment delay of a node v i ∈ V is the time delay caused by a misalignment between the latest end time of pre(v i ) and the start time of v i .

A DAG task has a sequence λ = {v src , ..., v sink } that starts at v src and end at v sink while satisfying (v k , v k+1 ) ∈ E, which is called a complete path. The length of a path is the sum of the worst-case misalignment delay and worst-case callback execution time (CE i ) of nodes constituting a path. In case of the worst-case misalignment delay, we abbreviate to MD i in the rest of this paper. The longest complete path of a DAG task is referred to as the critical path λ * . Nodes in λ * are referred to as critical nodes, while other nodes are called non-critical nodes. Finally, we can define the length of a DAG task. Definition 2. The length of a DAG task τ k , denoted by L k , is the sum of the worst-case misalignment and worst-case callback execution time of its critical path.
div.formula: L k = ∀vi∈λ * (CE i + MD i )

div.head: IV. OPTIMIZATION METHODS
div.p: We propose three optimization methods for a ROS task. First, in subsection A, we derive the response time bound considering the misalignment delay and preemption delay caused by default routines. After that, we introduce an algorithm to obtain the optimal spinning period for each node. Next, subsection B proposes a method to improve performance in real-time scheduling situations based on the fact that ROS uses TCP/IP for communication. Finally, in subsection C, we propose an algorithm assigning priority to each node when multiple instances overlap.

div.head: A. Spin Rate Optimization
div.p: This subsection presents the new response time bound for ROS tasks. The new response time bound for ROS tasks is based on a work-conserving scheduler and assumes that instances of tasks do not overlap (i.e., single instance). The structure of the DAG, execution time, misalignment delay, and preemption delay all contribute to the overall response time of a ROS task. Previous studies have considered the structure of the DAG and the execution time of each node but not the misalignment delay [5]- [7], [9]. The misalignment delay is determined by the spinning period of each node as stated in Lemma 1. Note that the spinning period of v src is equal to T and its misalignment delay is always 0. The source node, typically a sensor node such as a LIDAR or camera, periodically receives data and transmits it to internal nodes.
Lemma 1. The misalignment delay caused by node v i ∈ V is upper bounded by its spinning period T i .
div.formula: MD i = 0, if v i = v src T i , otherwise
div.p: Proof. As mentioned in Definition 1, misalignment delay is a delay caused by a time difference between the start time of a node v i and the latest end time of pre(v i ). In the case of v src , since pre(v src ) does not exist, a misalignment delay does not occur. Suppose the misalignment delay of v i ∈ V \v src is longer than T i . Then there is at least one polling time of v i before v i starts execution. At this polling time, v i must start execution because all of pre(v i ) is completed. Since this is a contradiction, the maximum misalignment delay of v i is T i .

Our response time analysis approach is based on the discrimination of DE i for each node and the basic response time of a task, as depicted in Fig. 3. The response time encompasses the callback execution time, misalignment delay, and preemption delay caused by DE i . Here, the preemption delay can be understood as the interference caused by higherpriority tasks (DE i ) that always preempt callbacks.

To compute the basic response time resulting from CE i and MD i , we need to define a workload. Typically, a task's workload is the maximum time it takes to execute on a single-core processor. Previous works consider only the node's worst-case execution time (WCET) without accounting for misalignment delay [5], [6], [9], [12]. However, in ROS, the workload can be defined by treating the misalignment delay as the execution time so that there is no polling behavior. This approach yields a more conservative response time because other nodes can occupy the CPU during MD i in reality. This idea is applied consistently throughout the remaining formulas in this paper. Lemma 2. The maximum time to execute an instance of τ (τ k ) in a single-core processor is upper bounded by the W k .
div.formula: W k = ∀vi∈V (CE i + MD i )
div.p: Proof. If a node v i ∈ V executes for less than its CE i or if the misalignment delay of a node is less than MD i , it can enable its successor nodes to execute earlier. This condition is still satisfied even when multiple nodes meet their start condition simultaneously. Hence, the overall response time cannot exceed the above formula.

div.head: B. High ksof tirqd Thread Priority
div.p: As briefly described in Section I, each node in ROS is an independent process and acts as an asynchronous polling method that periodically checks messages. Since each node is a different process, a communication method between nodes is needed. The ROS system uses TCP/IP to send and receive messages. TCP/IP that provides end-to-end communication is a framework for organizing the set of communication protocols. In Linux systems, it is handled by the bottom half of the interrupt handler, called Soft IRQ.

In Linux systems, TCP/IP operates at a lower priority than real-time processes, leading to potential delays in message delivery between nodes. As an example, consider the graph 5 shows that node v 3 receives the message on time and executes its callback, but node v 2 does not. This leads to an additional delay when v 2 receives the message at the following polling time. This problem is more likely to occur when the CPU utilization is high. To address this, we give the ksof tirqd thread, which handles unserved software interrupts and processes TCP/IP in Linux systems, the highest real-time priority. This ensures the callback execution as soon as all pre(v i ) finish, regardless of message delivery delay. As a DAG task runs on a single platform, and ksof tirqd takes less time than individual nodes, its time is not considered when calculating the response time.

div.head: C. Multiple-Instance Aware Priority Assignment
div.p: The policy for assigning node priorities is crucial for improving response time. In ROS systems, all messages are processed on the same nodes, making it difficult to determine which instance the incoming message belongs to. Additionally, dynamically changing node priority is expensive. Therefore, we use a static node priority assignment algorithm. Intuitively, the prior instance with smaller k should run earlier than the following instances to reduce worst-case response time. Conventional algorithms prioritize nodes close to v src , which prevents the following nodes from not running due to precedence constraints. However, if multiple instances of τ run simultaneously, it can increase the response time because an instance with a higher instance number interferes smaller one. For example, in Fig 2 ,v 1 in τ j gets the highest priority because it is the source node. Therefore, τ j interferes with τ i and delays the finish time of τ i . If this situation is repeated, in the worst-case scenario, each time a new instance is created, the previous instance cannot run in the CPU and can eventually miss the deadline. This motivated us to think of an algorithm that prioritizes nodes in reverse topological order.

Algorithm 4 is a pseudo-code for determining the priority of each node. It takes the task's graph representation as input and the node's priority as output. First, the length of each node is calculated (Line 1). Here, the node's length is the length of the longest complete path through each node. Then, after selecting all nodes which do not have descendants in V , we assign the node's priority based on their length (Line 4-9). The node which has a longer length gets high priority. Finally, the selected nodes and their related edges are removed from V and E, respectively (Line 10-11). We repeat this process until there are no nodes in V (Line 3).

Algorithm 5 uses dynamic programming to compute each node's length, which is used in Algorithm 4. First, we sort the nodes by topological order (Line 1). Then, in line 2-7, we traverse the DAG nodes by topological order while computing the lf of each node. Here, lf (v i ) is the longest path length that starts from v src and ends at v i ∈ V . div.head: V. EVALUATIONS
div.p: In this section, we evaluate the performance of our optimization methods through four parts. First, in subsection A, we assess the improvement in end-to-end response time when each optimization method is applied. Then, we compare our spin rate optimization method to Park2022 (the only paper dealing with spin rate optimization) to prove its superiority [16]. Subsection C evaluates our node priority assignment algorithm by comparing it with the algorithm used in He2019 [7]. The experiments in these three sections are based on randomly generated DAG tasks, similar to the technique used in [9]. Lastly, in subsection D, we present the results of optimizing and running Autoware, an open-source ROS-based autonomous driving software, on an embedded board.

In this study, 100 directed acyclic graph (DAG) tasks were generated using the methodology described in [9]. The generator starts with a source node, adds subsequent layers of nodes and ends with a sink node. The maximum depth (number of layers excluding the source and sink node) is randomly chosen from a range of 3 to 7. The number of nodes in each layer is limited to a parallelism parameter of 4 in this experiment. The source node is connected to nodes in the first layer, and nodes in the last layer are connected to the sink node. Any remaining open-ended nodes are connected to nodes in other layers with a probability of 0.05, repeating the process until there are no more open-ended nodes. Execution times CE and DE are randomly assigned to nodes with each execution time falling within a range of 1ms to 40ms and 0.01ms to 0.03ms, respectively. This process is repeated until the total sum of CE falls within a range of 220ms to 280ms. Each node v i has a single callback function that is executed only when all messages have been received from pre(v i ).

div.head: A. Evaluation of the End-to-End Response Time
div.p: We use Intel i7-8700 CPU as a reference computing platform and execute ROS tasks on Linux with an additional PRE-EMPT RT patch. Furthermore, since we use a measurementbased method that executes a ROS task on the CPU rather than simulation, we isolate only 4-cores out of 12-cores for accurate evaluation. A process with higher priority always preempts a lower priority process and processes with the same priority run in a round-robin scheduling policy with a 1ms time slice.

In this experiment, there are two parts: single-instance and multiple-instance. In the single-instance scenario, T src is set to 1s so that instances do not overlap. In the multiple-instance scenario, T src is set to 100ms so that multiple instances running simultaneously. In order to evaluate the performance improvement from each optimization method, the experiment was conducted with 8 cases for single-instance and 8 cases for multiple-instance, for a total of 16 settings. The response time was measured by running each DAG task for 25 seconds, eight times, and taking the worst-case value. div.p: When evaluating single-instance cases, the highest performance is achieved when only spin rate optimization is applied, reducing the response time to 0.36 times the unoptimized value. It is noteworthy that other optimization techniques do not improve performance but rather increase the worst-case response time. This is because optimization methods B and C are more suitable for multiple-instance cases than singleinstance ones. Our proposed priority assignment algorithm gives higher priorities to subsequent nodes considering the overlapping instances, which results in increasing the length of the single instance. In this case, it is practical to use techniques such as [7] and [9], which have been studied extensively. In addition, in the current single-instance experimental setting, TCP/IP does not have to be processed first because there are relatively large available rooms left on the CPU. Although we ignored the time consumed by TCP/IP, in real-world environments, the execution of each node is interfered with TCP/IP, resulting in an additional misalignment delay. Therefore, as seen in Fig. 6(a), without spin rate optimization, the response time increases by almost 1.5 times.

In the multiple-instance case evaluation, all three optimization techniques showed improved performance. The best results were achieved when optimization A and optimization C were applied together, reducing the worst-case response time to 0.37 times the unoptimized value. The application of optimization B and C improved performance, but when both were applied together, performance slightly decreased on average. To understand this, we analyzed the best performance setting for each task and categorized them as Table I based on their response time. For instance, 80% of tasks near 0.12s in response time have the best performance when optimization A and C are applied simultaneously. Here, the response time is an actual value in seconds, not a normalized value. Since the spinning period of v src is fixed to 100ms, the overlapping interval between the instances increases as moving to the right in the table. From the result, as the overlapping interval between instances increases, the ratio of optimization C, in this case, the sum of A+C and A+B+C in Table I, decreases. On the contrary, the ratio of optimization B, the sum of A+B and A+B+C, increases as the response time increases.

The intuition behind the observation is that with an increased portion of overlapped intervals, the number of nodes that have to run callback increases. In the case of a single instance, a relatively small number of nodes perform a callback simultaneously because the nodes are executed step by step from the earlier nodes. However, if multiple instances overlap, each instance wants to run different parts of the DAG. For example, in Fig. 2, τ i wants to execute nodes from v 6 to v 9 , but τ j wants to execute nodes from v 1 to v 5 in the overlapping interval. Therefore, it increases the need for TCP/IP to run first. Contrariwise, if the overlapping intervals are small, the effect of missing polling time increases due to the time to execute TCP/IP, as in single-instance cases.

Next, the structure of the DAG significantly affects optimization C. Since the sum of the total CE is restricted to a specific range in our experiment, tasks with a short response time have more parallelizable nodes, while tasks with a long response time have deeper layers. Tasks with many parallelizable nodes put a strain on the limited number of cores, reducing the ability to run new instances. Tasks with a deep depth, however, have less need to run preceding instances first as there are enough cores to run a new instance. Thus, the optimal setting varies based on the instance length and DAG structure, making it important to choose an optimization method considering these factors.

div.head: B. Effectiveness of the Proposed Spin Rate Optimization Technique
div.p: In this experiment, our proposed spin rate optimization algorithm is compared with the existing spin rate assignment technique. Park2022 assumes a round-robin scheduling and minimizes the critical length by complete search. Starting from the source node, it finds the spinning period of critical nodes that makes the critical length shortest by considering all possible spinning periods. Here, we assign each node a period in the range of 0.2ms to 100ms. It focuses on reducing the critical length rather than the overall response time because it assumes that the callback functions of each node are separate for each message and that the critical nodes play the most crucial role among the nodes. For a fair comparison, we use the same experiment setting and tasks used in subsection V.A.

The results of comparing our proposed spin rate optimization algorithm and the existing spin rate assignment technique (Park2022) are shown in the first row of Table II. The comparison is made based on single-instance cases where no optimization has been applied, and optimization B and C are not considered to see only the effect of spin rate optimization. The results show that while Park2022 reduces the response time by 30% on average, our algorithm is almost half as short. This indicates that our algorithm is more effective. Additionally, Park2022 is only applicable to round-robin scheduling systems, but our algorithm has a broader scope, covering other scheduling policies. Furthermore, Park2022's assumption that the critical chain solely determines the system performance is not valid for general DAG tasks.

div.head: C. Effectiveness of the Proposed Node Priority Assignment Technique
div.p: In this subsection, our proposed node priority assignment algorithm is compared against the start-of-art priority assignment algorithm. He2019 assigns the priority of each node while satisfying two properties. First, they assign priorities to nodes in the topological order (or descending order), which means a node can get priority after all of its ancestor nodes have been assigned priority. It is contrary to our proposed algorithm, which assigns priority in reversed topological order. Second, as in our proposed algorithm, they assign nodes with longer l(v i ) higher priorities. The same settings and tasks were used as in previous experiments.

The priority assignment algorithm is compared only for multiple-instance cases, as its main focus is to handle such cases. In addition, spin rate optimization was applied to create a more hard situation. In other words, the baseline of multiple-instance cases and Ours in the second row of Table II corresponds to A and A+C in Fig. 6, respectively. In the case of He2019, the result shows that the performance is improved by about 9 percent over the basic setting because it effectively reduces the length of an instance while quickly satisfying the execution conditions of each node. Our algorithm has improved performance by about 20% because it is possible to reduce the worst-case and average response time by executing the previous instance first. As we described in subsection V.A, our algorithm is ineffective for single-instance cases. However, in situations where multiple instances overlap, our algorithm can be more effective than conventional algorithms.

div.head: D. Implementing Autonomous Software on Board
div.p: Our proposed algorithms are shown to be effective on realworld software, using an Nvidia Jetson AGX Xavier with an 8-core Armv8.2 64-bit CPU and Linux PC with Intel i7-8700 CPU. The Xavier runs Autoware in a Linux environment with PREEMPT RT patch, while the Linux PC runs a real-time simulation in the simulated physical environment provided by SVL [2], [18]. The response time was measured during a simple lane-keeping scenario while isolating 4-cores out of 8-cores to eliminate interference from other processes. Fig. 7 shows the DAG structure of Autoware [2]. The lidar republisher node publishes LIDAR data every 100ms and serves as the source node, while the twist gate node functions as the sink node. Table III displays the measurements of CE i and DE i for each node on the Xavier board. Most nodes have a longer CE i than DE i , but planning nodes like op global planner, op trajectory generator, and op behavior selector have the same length. This is due to the fact that they only receive messages and finish the callback routine in a brief manner.

Since Autoware has a deep DAG structure with few parallelizable nodes, spin rate optimization and TCP/IP optimization were applied without assigning priority to the nodes (refer to subsection V.A). In the baseline setting, planning nodes had a low spinning period while other nodes had a high spinning period, but this was changed in the optimization results to give the planning nodes a high spinning period as they had a relatively large DE i (Table III). In Fig. 7, solid lines represent critical nodes, and dotted lines represent non-critical nodes. Table IV shows end-to-end response time results by running a simulation. The average response time and worstcase response time before optimization are considerable but reduced by nearly half after optimization. This shows that our algorithm not only improved the average performance but also the worst-case scenario, which is critical in real-time systems. In this paper, we propose optimization techniques aimed at reducing the response time of ROS, a widely used tool in robotics. Our methods consist of three optimizations: (i) spin rate optimization, (ii) high ksof tirqd thread priority, and (iii) multiple-instance aware priority assignment. Our experiments, using both randomly generated tasks and real-world software with simulation, show that our approach effectively reduces the average and worst-case response time of tasks. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper to propose a mathematical optimization method for the response time that considers misalignment delay and handles overlapping multiple-instance cases. In future work, we will focus on a detailed response time analysis for multiple-instance cases to achieve accurate spin rate optimization.
